newsitem.title: USA: Bombing judge denies media petitions on jurors.
newsitem.headline: Bombing judge denies media petitions on jurors.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Saturday denied a media request to release information about jury selection conducted behind closed doors, saying he was concerned about the safety and the privacy of jurors.

"People who come and serve on a jury do not come here for a strip search of their psyche and the press does not have a warrant to it," Federal Judge Richard Matsch said during an unusual Saturday session.

Matsch also refused to remove a shield that partially hides jurors serving in the high-profile case and said he would rule later on whether to remove or modify a sweeping gag order on the attorneys in the case.

Matsch made it clear he was not concerned about the jurors' safety because of defendant Timothy McVeigh who is accused of the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City that killed 168 people.
McVeigh has pleaded not guilty and faces the death penalty if convicted.
"There's always the possibility of someone seeking to make a claim to fame by (doing) something sensational," Matsch said.
Matsch disclosed that messages he has received about the case were "considerably different from messages of friendly persuasion." He did not elaborate.

During the 16 sessions of jury selection, some 99 prospective jurors were interviewed by the judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys on a wide range of subjects including their views on the death penalty.

But they were also asked detailed questions on their personal lives and their financial affairs. Some of the answers were heartbreaking to listen to, such as a parent speaking about the death of a teenage son or a woman giving up a child born out of wedlock.

The judge said a panel that partially hides the jury box was needed to help jurors focus on the witness box and not pay attention to a discreetly placed camera that allows telecasts of the proceedings via a closed-circuit to Oklahoma City where victims and relatives of those who died in the bombing can view it.
When media attorney Kelli Sager suggested the screen be removed during a weekend so the trial will not be interrupted, Matsch shot back: "You're not familiar with government contractors."

McVeigh's attorney Stephen Jones who, along with the media, was seeking a modification of the gag order, told the judge that recent published reports alleging his client confessed to the bombing make it necessary for him to respond at times. "In fairness, no one else speaks for Mr. McVeigh, but me," Jones said.
The judge who said he would rule later on the gag motion, said he did not want attorneys in the case being "spin artists" with the media.

On Friday nine prosecution witnesses testified, including a mother who lost her 16-month baby who was in the day-care centre in the Murrah building. Testimony on the immediate aftermath of the bombing resumes Monday morning.
